passA.summary: Ramana Siddanth Emani, a data scientist at Auditoria AI, argues that the limiting factor on shipping production AI agents is not model capability, GPUs, or frameworks — all of which improve on their own every few months — but the velocity of the developer's own inner loop. He lays out four harness primitives (parallel sub-agents in git worktrees, skills as organizational 'secret recipes', MCP connections to third-party systems, and a single-pane minimal UX) and walks a nine-step bug-fix pipeline from Jira ticket to staged deploy, claiming a human is genuinely needed only at steps 1 and 9. Part two pushes further: use recursive self-improvement, where you run the loop for a few days, ask the agent to enumerate its own bottlenecks, and remove them daily until a one-sentence prompt ships a fix end to end. He grounds this in finance, where SOX compliance and human sign-off make 'move fast and break things' untenable, and lands on the thesis that the human should remain a verifier but never the throughput ceiling. Worth watching if you're designing internal agent harnesses and want a concrete orchestration pattern; it's a short, opinionated talk with more assertion than measurement.
key_points: Demos are cheap and models, chips, and frameworks all improve on a predictable cadence, so the real differentiator in getting agents to production is how fast your developer loop iterates.
Sub-agents should run in parallel git worktrees — isolated folders — so that concurrent agents doing independent tasks don't fight over the same files.
The speaker claims a 48 GB MacBook can sustain roughly 50 active worktrees, i.e. 50 sub-agents working independently, with each QA-reported Jira ticket mapped to its own worktree.
Skills encode an organization's proprietary workflows and customer-specific recipes, ensuring agents follow the correct internal procedure rather than improvising a fix.
In a nine-step pipeline (parse ticket → RCA → pull traces/logs → TDD → fix → local e2e → PR → merge → dev/stage deploy), humans are only needed at the first and last steps.

Orchestration overhead is itself a bottleneck: multi-monitor context switching costs 'neck rotations', so the talk advocates collapsing dashboards, logs, Jira, PRs, and the coding session into one macOS widget.

Recursive self-improvement of the harness — run the loop for a day or two, have the agent list every bottleneck it hit, then remove them daily — compounds into near-autonomous bug fixing within about a month.

Combining goals with loops, plus a background 'dreaming' pass that compacts recurring customer session patterns into reusable data points, is how the speaker proposes removing the human from the loop entirely.
Finance raises the accountability bar: agent-reviewing-agent breaks the auditor/controller sign-off model that SOX compliance assumes, so the human verifier can't simply be deleted.

notable_quotes.text: So, how do we in real time fix these production bugs? The answer is your dev loop velocity.
notable_quotes.why: The thesis of the talk in one line.

notable_quotes.text: Always have the human as a verifier, but not the throughput ceiling because human attention is very limited.
notable_quotes.why: The closing formulation of the human's proper role, and the sharpest statement of the title's argument.

notable_quotes.text: Is it the model? Do you need a better model? Fable 5, perhaps? Or do you need faster GPUs?
notable_quotes.why: Frames the false diagnoses the talk exists to reject.

notable_quotes.text: If you wait 3 and 1/2 months, we are awarded with a new model in the market.
notable_quotes.why: Puts a number on why model capability isn't the lever worth pulling.

notable_quotes.text: The model capability increases very exponentially. And the developers have to spend a lot of time every day to automate your developer loop.
notable_quotes.why: States the asymmetry between free model progress and effortful harness progress.

notable_quotes.text: With you as the orchestrator, you can have, let's say, with 48 GB of RAM on your MacBook, you can have 50 active work trees.
notable_quotes.why: The talk's one concrete capacity number for parallel sub-agents.

notable_quotes.text: You don't want to queue up your tasks because the agent is will do that a lot better than you.
notable_quotes.why: A direct tradeoff claim: hand scheduling to the agent, not the human.

notable_quotes.text: So, I would say the human is only required at steps 1 and 9 because the in-between steps, the agent can do a lot better work.
notable_quotes.why: The specific, checkable claim about where human contact belongs in the pipeline.

notable_quotes.text: Second, we have skills. These are your organization secret recipes. So, make sure you have a lot of skills
notable_quotes.why: Defines skills as proprietary workflow encoding rather than generic prompting.

notable_quotes.text: So, all of us know production bugs are very high and production guards built by the hour.
notable_quotes.why: Sets up the demo-to-production gap the harness is meant to close.

notable_quotes.text: Where do you keep the accountability? If something goes wrong in production, you can't say Cloud is doing this. Something is wrong.
notable_quotes.why: The accountability objection to agent-reviews-agent in regulated domains.

notable_quotes.text: What is the bottleneck? It becomes a human attention because you yourself have to orchestrate all these different tasks.
notable_quotes.why: Names the bottleneck the title alludes to.

notable_quotes.text: moving fast and breaking things in sector in the finance sector is a lot different
notable_quotes.why: Marks where finance diverges from generic startup agent advice.

notable_quotes.text: So, you can see from the graph also, the number of neck rotations to ship one change like reduces a lot drastically.
notable_quotes.why: Memorable, if informal, metric for the cost of multi-window orchestration.

notable_quotes.text: At the end of one month, let's say, you have a really nice self-automated loop where you just type in one sentence and just say fix this bug for me.
notable_quotes.why: The concrete payoff claim for recursive harness self-improvement, with a timeline.

notable_quotes.text: you let the agent dream like humans dream in the background so that it collects all the sessions that your customers are using
notable_quotes.why: Introduces the 'dreaming' idea — offline compaction of usage patterns into reusable state.

notable_quotes.text: the developers do a lot of variety things in their software development life cycle and sitting behind a desk from 9:00 to 5:00 and just writing code is not valid anymore
notable_quotes.why: The implied claim about what the developer role becomes once the loop is automated.

notable_quotes.text: And you just compress all of this into one pane of glass because minimal UX is the key.
notable_quotes.why: Summarizes the UX primitive as a first-class part of the harness, not a nicety.

notable_quotes.text: So, sorry for the rude title. I don't mean to call the audience here the bottlenecks, but I'm here to talk about the harnesses that you guys are developing
notable_quotes.why: Scopes the talk to internal harness engineering rather than agent product design.

positions.claim: Production agent failures are caused by slow developer loops, not by insufficient model capability, GPU speed, or framework choice.
A new frontier model arrives roughly every 3.5 months and new chips roughly every year, so waiting on capability is a worse investment than automating your loop.
A MacBook with 48 GB of RAM can run about 50 active worktrees, i.e. 50 sub-agents in parallel.
In a nine-step bug-fix-to-stage pipeline, human contact is only necessary at step 1 and step 9; the agent does the intermediate steps better than a human.
Developers should not manually queue tasks for agents, because the agent schedules its own work better.
Consolidating dashboards, logs, tickets, PRs, and the coding session into a single widget measurably reduces the context-switching cost of shipping one change.
Agent-to-agent code review is inadequate in finance because accountability cannot be assigned to the model when something goes wrong in production.
Iteratively having the agent enumerate and remove bottlenecks in its own harness yields a one-sentence-prompt bug-fixing loop within about a month.
Background 'dreaming' — compacting recurring customer session patterns into data points the system reuses — is a viable mechanism for agent self-upgrade.
The human should remain a verifier of agent work but must never be the throughput ceiling of the system.
Writing code is now cheap enough that shipping impressive demos carries almost no signal about production readiness.
The traditional 9-to-5 desk-bound code-writing developer role is obsolete once agent loops are automated.
